speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SPREAD BETWEEN PRICE PAID PRODUCER AND COST TO CONSUMER
speechtext:
That a select standing committee of eleven members of the house be appointed to inquire into and investigate the causes of the large spread between the prices received for commodities by the producer thereof, and the price paid by the consumers therefor; the system of distribution in Canada of farm and other natural products, as well as manufactured products, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, more particularly to inquire into and investigate,

(a)	the effect of mass buying by department and chain store organizations upon the regular retail trade of the country, as well as upon the business of manufacturers and producers;
(b)	the labour conditions prevailing in industries supplying the requirements of such department and chain store organizations, and the extent, if any, to which existing conditions have been brought about by the purchasing practices of such organizations, and the effect thereof upon the standard of living amongst those employed in such industries and organizations;
(c)	the relation between the flour milling industry and the bakeries of the country, and the effect of such relations upon the baking industry of Canada;
(d)	the methods and system prevailing in the marketing of live stock and animal products for domestic consumption and export, and the extent to which the present system affords or restricts opportunity for fair returns to producers.
That the committee shall have power to send for persons, papers, and records, and the further power to request the appointment of a commission or commissioners under the Inquiries Act, to secure evidence to be presented to the committee by such commission or commissioners.
That the committee shall report to the house from time to time its findings, together with recommendations of such measures as in the opinion of the committee may be considered necessary to secure as far as possible, fair and just practices in the distribution and marketing systems of Canada, with fair and just returns to producers, employees, and employers, not inconsistent with the rights of consumers.
He said: The purposes to be served by the committee are, I think, amply indicated in the motion which I now move. I should not think it desirable at this time to enter into any discussion as to the correctness or otherwise of representations that have been made with respect to the causes for the great spread between the cost of commodities to the consumer and the price received by the producer. I think that might be regarded as an effort to pre-judge the case, and I

Price Spreads-Mr. Bennett
prefer to leave it without making any observations as to specific instances. Suffice it to say that I think it is probably well known to most of us that there is a wide spread between the prices received by the producers and the prices paid by the consumers of most commodities, natural and otherwise, with which we have to deal in the country.
The question of the retail trade in the country has received much attention during recent months. One of the trade journals has made very strong observations as to the necessity of having the business of mass buying by large organizatinos in some way regulated, but whether or not that is possible I am not expressing an opinion. I only indicate that the matter has been very forcibly presented to the public in recent months, and it is desirable that the whole subject should be investigated.
It will be recalled by this house that after the war a conference was held, in accordance with the terms of the treaty of Peace, looking towards more equitable provision being made for compensation for labour, better hours, less onerous, shall I say, hours of service, and better compensation. In this country the acute division of legislative powers between the Dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures has occasioned much diseussion, but most of the provinces did pass minimum wage acts and regulations were made under the provisions of those statutes. It is alleged, and very strongly, that there has been practically a disregard of the provisions of those statutes in many of the provinces and that industries and factories have been placed upon the exempt list with very evil consequences to those who are emplo3'ed in them. Without in any sense indicating the correctness or otherwise of the statements that have been made, the government has thought it desirable that there should be a close and careful consideration of all these matters as they affect the standard of living, compliance with the general principles of the law and the conclusions which were reached at the end of the war and embodied in the treaty of Peace and which in'fact brought about the maintenance at Geneva of an international labour bureau to which we have made notable contributions.
With respect to one particular industry in this country to which I observe reference was made yesterday by an hon. member from Saskatchewan regarding the relation between the bakeries and the milling industry, it is necessary for me at this moment only to remark that many of our milling industries own bakeries as subsidiaries and that the effect that such ownership has had upon the
price paid for bread or other products of the bakeries is a matter that will be considered by the committee.
The other problem to be dealt with is one that is almost a perennial, that is, how the marketing of live stock and animal products in this country may be improved. The other evening I pointed out that an effort had been made many years ago to improve conditions in Canada and that successive governments, federal and provincial, had endeavoured to graipplle with the question. The committee will investigate the method and system prevailing and ascertain to what extent the present system affords the largest possible opportunity or restricts the largest possible return being given to the producers. After consideration I thought it was not desirable to enter into a discussion of specific instances, because that might be regarded as a tendency to prejudge the matter, but I realize that to set up a committee of this kind it is necessary that witnesses should be called, that papers and documents should be examined, and that the committee should have before it evidence as to hours of labour, wages paid, and conditions. That is very difficult for any committee to secure by the mere calling of witnesses and it has been thought that the committee might direct that a commission be issued to some competent person to make inquiries in factories A, B, C and D and report such conditions to the committee. I believe that would serve the purpose without undue expense, and at the same time give first-hand evidence to the committee of the conditions about which complaints have been made. I know hon. members are all familiar with the use of the word "sweatshop" and recently representations have been made to me, and, I fancy, to hon. members opposite as to conditions in some of the factories of the country. It is proposed by this method, if it meets with the approval of the chamber, to deal with the situation, that is, that the committee shall determine that a given individual who has the qualifications necessary shall be appointed to make investigations into factories in Ontario, Quebec or elsewhere and then come back to the committee and report conditions as they are found. I do not think there is anything I desire to add beyond what is stated in the motion itself and these few preliminary observations which are made in explanation of the reasons for the motion being moved.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SPREAD BETWEEN PRICE PAID PRODUCER AND COST TO CONSUMER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
am rising, not to take exception in any way to the purpose to be served by the motion,

Price Spreads-Mr. Mackenzie King
namely, that of establishing a special committee of the house to make the inquiry indicated in the motion itself, but rather to express surprise that the government has waited until the fifth session of this parliament to introduce a motion of this kind.

subtopic: SPREAD BETWEEN PRICE PAID PRODUCER AND COST TO CONSUMER
speechtext:
How long did the
right hon. gentleman wait?

subtopic: SPREAD BETWEEN PRICE PAID PRODUCER AND COST TO CONSUMER
speechtext:
If we waited any 'length of time, it only makes the time hon. members opposite have waited still longer. If, before the late government went out of office, my hon. friends recognized the necessity for an inquiry into the matter referred to, I am more than ever surprised that they h$ve waited so long. The point I wish to make is that, ever since this parliament has been in session, there have been persistent representations as to the necessity for an investigation into the spread of prices; and into the necessity not merely for an investigation but for action by way of legislation which would make more effective legislation already on the statutes, and to meet a most pressing and urgent situation in the country.
The motion indicates that there is to be an inquiry by a committee with the possibility of the matter being followed still further by a royal commission. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has just indicated that in all probability a royal commission will be appointed. I would take that to mean that so far as this session of parliament is concerned, if we are to judge by the length of time parliamentary committees and royal commissions usually take to do their work, we shall hardly be able to look for much in the way of legislation that will help effectively to meet what apparently at last the government recognizes to be a very serious condition. The motion is in large part one of postponing action. What the country is interested in is not so much further inquiry with respect to matters about which nearly everyone knows a great deal, but legislation, if more is required, to meet a situation that is already understood.
Among motions specifically related to the question of inquiring into the spread of prices, was one introduced and discussed at the last session. In the course of the debate information was disclosed amply sufficient to guide the government in the matter of the necessary legislation. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) at the 'beginning of last session gave notice of the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, an immediate inquiry should be made under the provisions of The Research Council Act, chapter 177, R.S.C., 1927, or by other means, into the causes underlying the wide spread between the prices of raw products and the
IMr. Mackenzie Kinir.1
prices of goods manufactured from such products.
That resolution stood on the order paper throughout the greater part of the session. Finally, a debate took place upon it, and at that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), who has recently 'been speaking on this subject, said that later on he would have some observations to make on the subject in this house which would be- and I quote his words-"sympathetic and not in any sense antagonistic to the object they have in view." Why did not the Minister of Trade and Commerce come along with his further observations before the session was over? Nothing more was heard about the lesolution. It was allowed to remain on the order paper, the government gave no further opportunity to have it discussed. Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce now says that at that time he was in sympathy with the resolution. I submit that in view of the discussion which took place on that resolution, the government might well have held an inquiry during the recess and had legislation in readiness at this time, rather than to be now asking the house to appoint a special committee to begin inquiry.
Last night, in this chamber, an address was delivered by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) which showed as conclusively as any inquiry that could be made by a committee of this house the necessity for further legislation to meet the obvious restraints of trade and commerce which help to account for the wide spread between prices being paid to producers and those which are being paid by consumers.
I recall that this summer, speaking in western Canada, while in the province of Alberta, I drew the attention of the public to the necessity, perfectly obvious in the mind of every farmer I met while there, of some immediate investigation into what is believed by the cattle raisers to be a series of price fixing arrangements in connection with the processing of products of the cattle industry and of immediate legislation with respect thereto. I quote from a press dispatch from Claresholm, Alberta, of August 14, reported in the Ottawa Journal by Canadian Press, August 15, as follows:
"I find," said the Liberal leader to his Claresholm audience, "that people in the cattlebreeding business here are just 'being strangled in matters of trade."
In the combine which he believed' existed there was circle after circle, each demanding its profit, so finally a great spread grew up between the producer and consumer.
It is not necessary to have any government inquiry to find out that that condition is

Price Spreads-Mr. Mackenzie King
existing, it is known by the cattle-raisers generally throughout western Canada. What I think was really to have been expected from the government at this time was, not that they should be asking the house, in this fifth session, to appoint a committee of inquiry, but that they would bring down concrete legislation in the light of information which hon. members already have, and which is ample for the purpose of guiding the government.
There is one other aspect which I think is perhaps even more important. It is that the government has already legislation available to deal with matters of this kind, if it will view the whole question sympathetically. Legislation is one thing, but the administration of existing law is quite another. I do not think one need go beyond what has taken place in the last three or four years to recognize very clearly that no matter what the laws may be, unless the department of the government that administers them is wholly sympathetic with the object in view, the law will serve very little purpose. We have on the statutes a Combines Investigation Act which provides all the machinery necessary for the purpose of making the fullest possible kind of inquiry into any matter preventing or lessening competition or restraining trade; effective machinery, machinery giving all the powers and affording as well all the safeguards needed in connection with inquiry into matters of this kind. But where inquiries have started under the Combines Investigation Act, as far as they have been within the control of the ministry proceedings have been protracted and permitted to drag along from year to year so that the legislation itself has been rendered largely ineffective. What is really needed is sympathetic administration.
To illustrate the difference between the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen opposite and that of hon. members on this side with respect to the investigation of combines, monopolies and other organizations in restraint of trade, I might point out that in 1910 the Liberal government of the day placed on the statutes a Combines Investigation Act. That statute served a useful purpose while the Liberal administration was in office. Soon after, the Conservative party came into power in 1911. In 1914, the war came on, and during the period of the war there were other matters to which attention of necessity had to be given, and some matters which were of great importance at other times did not at that time receive the same amount of attention. But long before the war was over, there was ample
evidence of the extent to which formidable monopolies and combinations in restraint of trade had been developing, which had been doing much to further the artificial fixation or control of prices. Did the government of the day try to proceed under the act? Did they not rather take a course quite the opposite? Hon. gentlemen will recall that they repealed the Combines Investigation Act, and substituted for it two other pieces of legislation; the Board of Commerce Act, passed in 1919, and a so-called Combines and Fair Prices Act passed in the same year. But these measures had no sooner been passed than their constitutionality was questioned, and shortly before the government of that day went out of office a decision was given by the judicial committee of the privy council to the effect that the Board of Commerce Act was ultra vires. In other words, all that was done was to repeal an act which was wholly effective, and substitute for it measures which would prevent any real investigation taking place meanwhile.
What happened after the change of administration? In 1923, the Minister of Labour in the late Liberal administration reintroduced a Combines Investigation Act. A great deal of study and care had been given to its preparation. A Combines Investigation Act was again placed on the statutes and while a Liberal administration was in office the measure was sympathetically administered. The public soon became aware of the fact that, if the attention of the Department of Labour were drawn to combines and monopolies in restraint of trade in accordance with the provisions of the act, a very thorough investigation might be expected. The result was that many of those who otherwise might have lent themselves to price fixing by agreements to restrict and hamper trade were more cautious and careful in their action. But since hon. gentlemen opposite have come into office the Combines Investigation Act has not been as sympathetically administered. Indeed, one has only to look at the estimates laid on the table by the bon. the Minister of Finance a day or two ago, to see how this very year, at this very moment, at a time when the act is more needed than ever before, and when its provisions should be of the greatest possible service, the government is actually cutting down the appropriation needed for efficient and effective administration of the act. I have in my hand the estimates of the Department of Labour for the year ending March 31, 1935. I find that in the year 1933-34 a total of $43,000 was appropriated for the purposes of the act, but that

Price Spreads-Mr. Mackenzie King
this year there is to be an appropriation not of $43,000 but of $22,000. The vote is practically cut in half, and this at a time when hon. gentlemen by the motion which they now introduce, concede the necessity for full inquiry into the sort of thing with which the Combines Investigation Act was enacted to deal.
May I add that the Combines Investigation Act contains within its provisions ample powers for all the investigation that need be made to guide the government in the matter of further legislation? The legislation is already there, we do not need to wait for a committee of this house to report on these matters. There is ample provision in the act for conducting inquiry if the government is really in earnest.
Take one matter that the Prime Minister has just referred to, the appointment of a royal commission. The Prime Minister says when this committee meets that possibly they will want some additional information, and that in all probability a royal commission will be appointed to secure the information. Why should it be necessary to take that step when the legislation I have in my hand has anticipated and provided the means to meet the need for that very sort of thing? Let me read section 12 of the Combines Investigation Act, 1923:
All provisions of the Inquiries Act not repugnant to the provisions of this act shall apply to any inquiry or investigation under this act, and the registrar and every commissioner shall have all the powers of a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act, including the powers mentioned in section 11 thereof, whether thereunto authorized by the commission issued in the case or not, except in so far as Slid: powers may be inconsistent with the provisions of this act.
With all the powers that could be conferred under the Inquiries Act, under which royal commissions are appointed, already given the commissioner under this measure; with those powers available to the minister in order to obtain the information that is necessary to guide parliament or his department, why should there be need for a royal commission? More than that, on his own initiative the minister can hold an inquiry into any one of the various matters mentioned in the provisions of the act. He has a staff that is efficient and trained in matters of this kind, and he has a registrar who has shown his capacity for careful, tactful, thorough and efficient investigation. Why should an effort be made to get out from under this act, in an investigation of this kind, and have matters placed in the hands of a royal commission?

In a word, Mr. Speaker, that is my objection, so far as I have any, to the motion before the house at the moment. I would not in any way discourage any step which will help arouse the ministry to the necessity for action, but I do say that they ought to be fully aroused at the present time, that they ought to have been fully aware of the need for inquiry long ago and that they ought to have been fully aware of the need for what more may be required in the way of legislation. I say the ministry ought now to be prepared with its legislation. Just about this time last year, speaking in this house, I pointed out that if there were, as I thought possible, limitations to this act in coping with new situations which have arisen, the government ought to supplement it by additional legislation. I said that the Combines Investigation Act was only a beginning. I quote from what I said on February 27, 1933:
The Combines Investigation Act is but a mere beginning and does not meet the situation obtaining to-day. There should be more adequate facilities for investigations, and additional penalties should be imposed. Some conditions obtain which should be remedied by additional provisions in the criminal code. To-day we are seeking in vain to cope with these evils by milder methods.
Why are not additional provisions recommended for the criminal code in order to meet some of the situations which I think are pretty obvious and understood by the public generally? The public are looking at this session not for further inquiry or further royal commissions but for action in the nature of legislation.
I have just one further thought to add, and it is this: Since the government has decided that a parliamentary committee is advisable for the purpose of inquiry, the government should enlarge the scope of the inquiry in a manner which will go to the very root of the situation. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have drawn attention to what they have referred to as mass purchasing and alleged evils growing out of mass purchases in the retail and wholesale trade. When purchases are made they are made from large manufacturing concerns, and when large manufacturing concerns fix their prices for the things they sell they take into account all items that have entered into the cost of production. I submit that what is really required, above everything else, is an inquiry into the methods of financing of some of the large industrial concerns of this country, and what through reckless financing has been occasioned by way of loss which is being passed on to the consumer and for which the consumer is paying to-day.

Price Spreads-Mr. Marcil
That is a situation, Mr. Speaker, of the existence of which we have had ample evidence south of the line, and anyone who .is familiar with conditions in Canada will realize that a similar situation exists here. So I would suggest that, before this motion carries, if at all possible, it should be enlarged to include an investigation into the method of financing of some of this country's industrial concerns.
Mr. WILLIAM G. ERNST (Queens-Lunenburg) :	Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask
the Prime Minister if he would consider an amendment to paragraph (d) of the resolution. Probably in the case of no other commodity is there a greater spread between the price paid by the purchaser and the price paid to the producer than in the case of fish. Paragraph (d) may be intended to include an inquiry into the fish business, but that does not appear. So I would ask the Prime Minister if he would consider an amendment to that paragraph, inserting after the words " live stock " the word " fish," so that it would read, " in the marketing of live stock, fish and animal products."

speechtext:
When
coming to attend this session of parliament, Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take a very active part in the debates, but when I saw this motion which has been brought forward by the Prime Minister I could not help thinking that it should be enlarged. Holding that opinion I wish to suggest, and in fact I may say that I am going to move, an amendment as an addition to the motion before I resume my seat.
My reason for thinking that the motion does not go far enough in the matter of
investigation lies in the fact that no reference is made to the point I wish to raise. In paragraph (a) we have the matter of mass buying which is to be investigated; under paragraph (b) labour conditions are to be looked into; paragraph (c) deals with the relationship between the flour milling industry and the bakeries of Canada. These are all to be investigated, but there is one phase of the question of industrial development in Canada which I think should attract the attention of the government to a greater extent than the subjects I have mentioned, and that is the effect of the administration of the finances of this country upon industry in general.
The administration of our finances, as I understand the principle, should be so arranged as to serve industry and not have industry serve finance. It is a patent fact that within the last few years the financiers of Canada have developed industries to serve their own needs. Why should the bankers, brokers, those in charge of bondhouses, trustees or trust companies have the administration of Canadian industry? It is a known fact that one of the chief reasons for failure in the production of newsprint is that the financiers have encouraged kite flying to the very skies. Instead of pointing the way for the industries, attempting to effect a curbing influence, and pointing out that the industries are on dangerous ground, those financiers have encouraged development to the point where they, the financiers of Canada, the brokers, the trust companies and the banks have taken the personal profits to themselves, a process which has not been in the best interests of the industries affected.
The same statement would apply to the development of Canada's mineral resources, to our lumbering industry, and to many others I might name. I repeat that the time has come when this parliament should take the matter in hand and by legislation, and if necessary drastic legislation, prevent the financiers from in future handling the finances of Canada the way they have been handled in the past.
Probably the house would excuse me if to some extent I violate the rules and read from a manuscript. Why should we find industry being controlled by banks and trust companies? If the financiers had not encouraged promoters to fly their financial kites to the skies we would not have in Canada to-day such drastic failures. Let us if possible get to the bottom of the financial evil, and thus lay the foundation for more solid and enduring development of our industrial life. If we

Price Spreads-Mr. Heaps

can do this we will be sounding the death knell of industrial speculation, we will be securing a solid foundation for our internal expansion, we will secure better wages for our labouring class, we will put an end to uncontrolled and ruinous competition and, above all, we will lessen mass buying, of which there is so much complaint. Through this action organized industry will be able so to lessen its overhead and control its cost of manufacture that competition will find a common ground on which to make offerings of its wares to the public. Those who complain of mass buying cannot, and should not, blame the wholesale purchaser who knows that the manufactured goods offered to him are priced on the basis of the amount of watered stock which can be traced to their cost, the effect over-capitalization has had upon the cost of production, and the relation of high interest rates to such cost.
The firm that has not been cursed by such over-capitalization, watered stock and undue rates of interest can afford to sell at prices yielding a moderate profit. Is it any wonder that wholesale dealers will say to the manufacturers, "Your prices are too high, and unless vou come down to something reasonable we will have to purchase elsewhere,-outside of Canada, if necessary. We should not be called upon to pay an added cost arising from the fact that you have to pay from eight percent to twelve percent for the money you have borrowed. We should not be called upon to pay an added price caused by over-valuation or over-capitalization of your stock. We should not be called upon to pay the prices which you claim you must add to your ordinary profit to take care of the high rate of interest which you have to pay for the money invested in the development of your industry." Can you blame the wholesalers for mass buying? Can you blame a wholesaler when he states to a certain firm, "Your cost is too high, and if you do not come down to a reasonable price we will have to look elsewhere, even if we have to look outside of Canada." My conclusion is that the only way to remedy the evil I have outlined is to go fully into the whole matter, call upon our captains of industry, our banks, our trust companies and our brokers to lay bare, before a committee of the house, or, if you like, a royal commission, the methods adopted in their business transaction.
To that end I move the following and ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to add what I have to suggest as subsection (e) of his motion now before the house:
(e) the methods and system that have prevailed in the distribution of common stock,

preferred stock and the flotation of bonds by brokers, trust companies and banks for the development of industry in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to voice my endorsation of the motion now before the house. I feel inclined to believe that had the motion come from this corner of the house we might have been accused of attempting to upset some of our established institutions, and of reverting to socialistic and bolshevistic tactics. However, coming as it does from the government side of the house I suppose we may put it down as an act of statesmanship. Therefore I wish to commend the government upon its act of statesmanship in introducing the motion now before us.
My purpose in rising is to put a question to the government concerning a matter debated in the month of November, 1932. At that time I spoke concerning conditions of wages and labour in the textile industry. During the course of the debate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) rising in his place stated that the government was prepared to submit the whole question of wages and conditions in the textile industry to the tariff board, when that board had been appointed. The tariff board has been appointed, but I am not going to ask the Prime Minister to refer this subject to it. If the committee now under consideration is appointed, and no doubt it will be, would the Prime Minister tell me whether or not the question of labour conditions and wages received by those employed in the textile industry will come under the purview of the committee and whether such committee will be able to make a thorough investigation into conditions now prevailing in that industry?

Mr. Speaker, in the few remarks I wish to make it is not my intention to speak in opposition to the principle of the resolution. As a matter of fact I believe I may claim that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has adopted my child, because last year I moved a resolution along the lines of the present one. To-day it appears on the order paper as number 23 in the notices of motions. It would appear therefore that in this instance the government is just a year late in considering the matter. I do not know but what the government would be well advised to accept the resolution I have on the order paper instead of this one which the Prime Minister has placed before us because I believe that it is quite possible to accomplish what is desired a little sooner by my resolution than by this cumber-

Price Spreads-Mr. McKenzie
some method of first appointing a parliamentary committee to make an investigation with the hope of having it all completed in time for legislation to be passed at this session.
My reason for presenting my resolution in the first place a year ago was that, first of all, I thought of the farmers and the labouring people throughout the country who are in such dire distress owing to the present economic conditions, and because of those conditions, which still prevail, it is surely time that the farmers who produce wheat, for instance, should be able to get part at least of the profit that comes from the growth of that wheat. The farmer prepares the ground, sows the crop, reaps it and markets it, and after doing all that, he makes the least of anybody who has anything to do with the handling of that wheat. I think that the time has come when the men who labour on the land should have an opportunity of making a decent living. The same thing that applied a year ago still applies to live stock, poultry and all the other farm products. I was thinking principally of farm products when I introduced my resolution a year ago.
The resolution which the Prime Minister has presented to the house deals in paragraph (a) with the effect of mass buying by departmental and chain store organizations; (b) deals with labour conditions; (c) deals with the flour milling industry and (d) with the methods prevailing in the marketing of live stock and animal products for domestic consumption and export. That probably goes far enough, but what I am concerned about is whether the matters which I brought to the attention of the house a year ago and the conditions I pointed out then as existing throughout the country will be fully gone into by this committee of inquiry,. When that committee meets, whoever may be on it, when some person introduces something along the lines I have just suggested here with regard to farm products, I do not want some member of the committee to reply that the scope of the committee's reference does not permit them to go that far, and thereby be precluded from introducing that subject.
I am concerned to know just what is behind the fact that the five and ten cents a pound which the producer gets for wool to-day becomes two dollar per pound clothing when it is processed, and why it is that hides that are selling for as low as fifty cents apiece are made into ten and twelve dollar boots, and equally expensive harness, sole 74726-13 i
leather, lace leather and other products. I want to know not only the facts about the flour milling industry but also why some of the breakfast foods that are so extensively used are so expensive to buy when grain is at its present low price. I want to know why it is that these conditions prevail and if the scope of this resolution and of the reference that will be made to the committee will allow of all these matters being taken up and investigated fully by the committee.
Last year I suggested that tariffs and combines were largely responsible for those conditions. My right hon. leader has dealt with the question of combines. I believe that tariffs and combines are largely responsible for the conditions that exist, and I should like to see that matter fully investigated.
I believe, as has been stated before, that there is considerable to be investigated in the textile industries in this country. My information is that the textile industries are fairly busy, but that the wages are lower than they have ever been before. If that is the case I think there should be an investigation into that industry.
I think inquiry should also be made whether or not there are industries in this country that should never have been given protection -exotic industries. If there are such, I for one am willing to let those industries be discontinued if they are costing us more through their tariff protection and the high prices they are charging for their products than they are returning to us in salaries and services.
During the last two years the expression has been widely used in this country-Buy made-in-Canada goods. We remember that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr1. It is perhaps one of the most complex and intricate tasks any government has undertaken. The same thing obtains here, perhaps in a lesser degree, because this country is not so large and its businesses are not so extensive. section (d), where the live stock industry is promised to be looked into. Some of the members of the government will recall that when they came into power they found the sum of $25,000 already voted for this very purpose by their predecessors. The vote did not get there all by itself; it was put there for a purpose, and I hoped that the government would take advantage of it and hold the inquiry which had been anticipated by their predecessors. However, they either used the money for some other purpose or let it lapse into the treasury. They did not proceed with the inquiry. On the principle that it is better late than never, I approve of this action on the part of the government, particularly with regard to live stock.
With regard to subsections (a) and (b), affecting the chain stores, it was inevitable that the government should take action if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) were not going to be let down as a gentleman engaging in heroics before the country with the idea of obtaining some approval, which he did get. I can bespeak one class of people who will approve of this action, namely, the very much embarrassed retail traders throughout Canada, especially in the small villages in the west. They are at their wits' end to know how to carry on. What with the competition of the buses, and the drays and the highways, the mail order houses and the chain stores, and competition among themselves, they hardly know what line of goods to keep which they can dispose of to advantage. I know the minister will get sympathy from these people.
Just how the minister is going to investigate and put a stop to mass buying I do not know. Perhaps we have been wrong in the past in our industrial development methods, but we have always thought that it was a good thing to conduct affairs efficiently, and that we should buy in large instead of in small quantities. The very foundation of industrial development has been to purchase our raw material cheaply. There is an old saying that anything that is bought properly is half sold, so that the buyer can buy it to advantage. I am sure our wives always like to go to the chain stores-why? Because they can get good bargains. Maybe while these things are so there are nevertheless some abuses. One or two have happened to come to my attention comparatively recently. The chain stores will acquire a line of farm produce, for example,

pigs' feet, which is a great dainty with some people. They will buy the whole output of an abattoir and use them as a drawing card for their customers, a sort of advertisement. Instead of spending so much money in newspaper advertising they use this line to serve the same purpose. This competes with the regular meat trade and it affects the price not only of pigs' feet but of almost every cut in the animal. So that the chain store business, with its ramifications, is enormous. Just how it can be remedied I do not know, but I wish my hon. friend good luck.
I do not know whether the minister has tackled something bigger than he realized, but he has certainly undertaken a tremendous proposition, and no one can do anything but wish him well in his remedial endeavours.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), if I understood him rightly he took credit for the milk investigation-and I do not want to discredit it; it was quite outside its jurisdiction but it did something, and something is always better than nothing as a rule-for having put Winnipeg wise as to how to solve the milk problem there. Yes, I shall deal with that
a little later. It seems to me that the vital question is not so much: What does the producer receive in dollars and cents for his product? but: What can he buy with that mone;1 when he gets it? If he receives, no matter what price for his product and then finds that the commodities he wishes to buy are at a price level he cannot reach, he is not assisted very much.
Not very long ago I w'as talking to a gentleman who had been farming in the west for many years. He told me that he had never been so well off as in the old days when wheat was selling at sixty to seventy cents a bushel; but, he said: "In those days I could buy a mower for fifty bushels of wheat and now the same mower costs me 200 bushels. In those days I could buy a binder for 250 bushels of wheat whereas now it costs 600 bushels. In those days I could buy a pair of overalls for a bushel and a half of wheat whereas now it would cost four bushels." The trouble to-day with our primary producers is that they have to pay so much for the products of the secondary industries that they are not able to buy them. Three or four years ago when this government took office, prices were declining rapidly throughout the world, and in particular prices of farm and natural products generally, and the government found itself pow'erless to stop this de-
Price Spreads-Mr. Young

oline. What was the logical thing for the government to do under the circumstances? It was to endeavour to see that all other prices came down along with the prices of primary products. But the government took the opposite view; they said: At least we can stop the prices of manufactured goods from coming down, and they legislated accordingly. They adopted a fiscal policy calculated to prevent a decline in the prices of manufactured goods commensurate with the decline in the prices of farm products. What was the result? In 1929 a dollar's worth of farm products in this country would buy a certain quantity of manufactured goods. In 1933 it required SI.62 worth of farm products to buy the same quantity of manufactured goods. That widening of the spread had the effect of putting our primary producers out of the market; they could not buy the products of the secondary industries.
We are now told that the mail order houses and chain stores follow unethical practices in their buying methods. It is generally conceded that the cost of merchandising goods, that is, of getting them from the producer to the consumer, is excessive. Perhaps that is due in large measure to the fact that we insist on too much in the way of service, or it may be to an expensive organization that we have for distributing goods. But the mail order houses were the first people to take a step in the direction of solving that problem; they were the first to help in reducing the spread between the price which the consumer pays and what the producer receives. This worked a hardship at the time on the local storekeeper. As a result he was driven to form chain stores and we have the mail order house and the local merchant organized into chain stores, buying now by a more economical method than that followed formerly and so bringing goods to the consumer at a lower cost than before. In that I think they are rendering a real service to the community.
Not many days ago something was said in the press about a speech delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), I think in Toronto, and one mail order house challenged him to prove that they had been guilty of unethical practices. If I recall rightly the instance he gave was something like this:	That company had
gone to a certain woollen mill in Scotland and offered them an order for some 250,000 yards of a certain kind of cloth at a price somewhat lower than the mill was asking. The mill at first refused to accept the price, but when the company's buyer went away saying: Very good, he reecived a telegram

a day or two later accepting the price. I cannot see anything unethical or wrong in that. Surely such a company has the right to bargain for those goods as best it can, and when it passes those goods on to the consumer with that saving of price, certainly the Canadian people are going to benefit. If you stop that kind oi thing, you say this, that prices must forever remain as they are; they must become rigid and never be lowered. It has been demonstrated beyond peradven-ture that the government is powerless to stop the decline in the price of natural products, those things that are sold on the world market. The logical thing to do then is to bring down the prices of other things proportionately so that people can buy them on an equal basis. But when you say that you will not allow the prices of certain commodities to come down, to share in the deflation, you are putting other classes in the community in the position where they cannot buy the products of those people. I think it was said by a witness in the milk inquiry last year that even if they got the milk for nothing, they would still have to charge seven cents a quart for it. What does that mean? It means that while the producer got nothing for his labour, certain other people had to have their full share. That is not equitable.
Let us read paragraph (a) of the resolution :
The effect of mass buying by department and chain store organizations upon-
Upon what?
-the regular retail trade of the country, as well as upon the business of manufacturers and producers.
Not a word about the consumer. Paragraph (b) reads:
The effect thereof upon the standard of living amongst those employed in such industries and organizations.
Nothing about the consumer. Paragraph (c) speaks of:
The relation between the flour milling industry and the bakeries of the country, and the effect of such relations on the baking industry of Canada.
Not a word about its effect on the price of bread. It seems to me that the essential thing is to look at the whole problem from the standpoint of the consumer. If you can get the goods into the hands of the consumer at a reasonable price, he will buy the goods and that will give employment to others. But if you pick out certain classes in the community, as is done in this resolution, and

Price Spreads-Mr. Reid
see that they do not suffer any reduction in their wages, the effect will be a rigiditf in the price level at certain points; it cannot be adjusted and the result will be that some people will not be able to buy the products of others. I hope the government in making this inquiry will not lose sight of the fact that the whole question should be studied from the standpoint of the consumer. Let me once more quote these words I have quoted before from Bastiat:
Study all economic questions from the consumer's standpoint for the consumer's interests are the interests of the human race.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution, so far as it goes, meets I believe with the unanimous approval of the house, but like some hon. members who have spoken I do not believe it goes far enough and I think this is the time when further suggestions should be made with a view to enlarging the scope of the inquiry.
I was particularly pleased to hear the subject of fish mentioned by some members on both sides of the house, and in that matter I would say that conditions peculiar to British Columbia fisheries are somewhat different from those prevailing in some other provinces. One hon. member spoke about one and one-half cents per pound being given to fishermen. The fishermen of the Fraser river were offered one cent for fish weighing from seven to ten pounds apiece. But, in the course of his remarks, the hon. gentleman said that there was a difference between the American legislation respecting trusts and combines and the Canadian Combines Investigation Act, in that the former American legislation was based upon opposition to combines as such, whereas the present legislation is based upon a recognition that combines are inevitable, and that it is rather at the abuse to which combines are likely to give rise than at combines as such that legislation is directed and for which remedies are provided.
I stated that when the Canadian Combines Investigation Act was introduced the position taken by the government at the time was that combinations as such should not be regarded as illegal, that the Canadian act differed in that particular from the legislation then existing in the United States; also that the same was true of the Combines Investigation Act which was reintroduced in 1923 in Canada. Both these enactments were based on the theory that this is an age of world-wide competition and that combination is inevitable and as such should not be regarded as of itself an evil. On the other hand, it was recognized that large combination makes for great power in the direction of affairs and that all such power involves the possibility of abuse. It was and is against the abuses of combinations that the Canadian Combines Investigation acts were framed.
It is much to the credit of Canada that the position which this parliament has taken from the outset with respect to combines should be (he one which, after some twenty-five years of legislation on the subject, the United States has come only this year to recognize as the right one. While, as the Prime Minister says, from the mere statement that an act is intended to have a certain purpose, it does not necessarily follow that that purpose is attained; nevertheless, where the provisions themselves bear out what is said, the statement with regard to its essential features made at the time of introduction of a measure does help to throw light on the matter. If that statement is not in any way questioned when the legislation itself is under review, it is a factor which must necessarily be taken into account in the construction of the statute.
I have in my hand the debates of January IS, 1910, at the time at which the Combines Investigation Act was introduced. Sir Robert Borden was then leader of the opposition, and Sir Robert asked for an explanation. I was, at the time, holding the position of Minister of Labour in the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and in reply to Sir Robert Borden I made, in part, the following statement:

This is an age of organization and not merely of local or national competition but of world-wide competition and any industry or any nation which wishes to hold its own in the field of competition must do much in the way of perfecting organization.

I desire only to correct some misapprehensions.
The common law of England declared in what was known as the Great Mogul steamship case, that all restraints of trade and associations are of course not illegal. Associations of farmers, of workingmen, of manufacturers, of producers, it mattered not who, were not illegal; and the common law to that effect still prevails largely in England. On the continent, of course, cartels are largely favoured. There are two world cartels that are very well known by all those who have to do with trade in these days; one has to do with chemicals and chemical products, and the other with steel. The one with respect to steel is perhaps not quite as effective as the one that has to do with chemicals. However, when it became apparent, shall I say, about the middle of the nineteenth century, that in new countries combinations were operating to the detriment of the consumer to such an extent that they could no longer be endured, legislation was passed by many countries. In the United States the Sherman Act was passed, aimed at ending combines. The Supreme Court of the United States dealt with the great tobacco case, and with the United States Steel case, under the Sherman Act, and with many cases that arose out of combinations in that country.
In this country, as the right hon. gentleman said, in 1910, while he was Minister of Labour, an act was introduced respecting combines that adopted the British common law principle, namely that all combinations were not illegal nor per se bad, but only if they had certain effects; one for instance being unduly enhancing prices, another unduly restraining trade-and very frequently the word "unduly" appeared in consequence of the recognition of the legality of combinations on the one hand and the desire to prevent them from bringing about an improper condition in the body politic on the other. There were two or three notable prosecutions in this country in the criminal courts under the provisions of our criminal code. One was in Brantford; one was against the grain exchange in Winnipeg; one was against the lumber combine in western Canada. When I was much younger than I am now I defended that action. I should like to correct my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) who, in his anxiety to blame the retaliatory action, as he called it, of the United States with respect to lumber upon some action that had been taken here, as usual lost his sense of perspective. The real truth is that the president of the United States, as is well known, was opposed to the action that was taken, and it is well known that the house was. But it is also well known that, the late Senator Jones succeeded by methods that he himself described at the moment in inducing the Senate to add to the tax bill of that time a provision whereby a tax of S3 per thousand feet was placed upon lumber that camp into the United States from British Columbia and elsewhere, and it was to expire at a given date. President Hoover was opposed to it and the house was opposed to it, but- the senate attached that tax provision to the measure, and rather than veto it and take the risk that was attendant upon such action as was stated in the public press at the time, the president allowed the measure to go into effect. There was no question of attaching blame upon the government for that action. The tax was imposed in that way, and it had no relation to any tariff legislation that took place 'here, for it was not tariff legislation itself. The result was what

speechtext: Last evening the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was not in his place when it was suggested that we would make a formal motion that the Speaker do leave the chair for the purpose of taking an item in supply in order to forward the business of the house and enable supply to be taken at a later date. The hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) directed my attention to the rule, which provides that the Speaker shall leave the chair on Thursdays and Fridays without question put. Obviously that is after he has left it for the first time, and my reading of the rule is that if a formal motion is made, that he do now leave the chair, which of course leaves the whole subject matter open for debate, he may do so on any day, whether it be Thursday or Friday. But after the house has gone into committee of supply, neither on Thursday nor on Friday will a motion be made; the Speaker will leave the chair, but no matter can be discussed in supply which has not been considered on a day other than Thursday or Friday. I think that is the correct interpretation.

I have been looking at what took place and I observe that the Prime Minister said that he was of the opinion a formal motion could be pult and the house could resolve itself into committee of supply.
I believe this would require unanimous consent on a Thursday or Friday, where no item in supply had been previously called. I should think otherwise there would have to be notice in advance of any motion. I should like to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to standing order No. 57, which reads:
The house will appoint the committees of supply and ways and means at the commencement of every session, so soon as an address has been agreed to, in answer to His Excellency's speech.

I think exception should have been taken, that the motion should not have been made until after the address to His Excellency had been agreed to. Having slipped that stage, if I may use that expression, I think we should hardly be justified in going a step further and again transgressing a rule, which evidently was intended to protect hon. members as regards adequate time in which to prepare for the subjects that are to come up for disoussion. Standing order No. 57
was considered when the motion was made by the Minister of Finance. We read the rule to mean that in any event the motion must be made as soon as the address has been agreed to, and cannot be deferred to a later day. But there is nothing to prevent its being made earlier. You set up your committee as soon as the house is in order; but in any event you must set it up as soon as the address has been agreed to in answer to His Excellency's speech. That is the construction which we put upon the rule, although that does not mean that it is correct. It was certainly, however, what we believed 74726-15
would be regarded as the reasonable interpretation to place upon it. The committee of ways and means and the committee of supply are committees that must be set up at the beginning of every session under our general system of procedure, and the rule means, we take it, that as soon as the address has been adopted it must be done in any event. subtopic: COMMITTEES OF SUPPLY AND WAYS AND MEANS BEFORE ADDRESS AGREED TO
speechtext:
That was what I tried
a moment ago to say to you, Mr. Speaker. Undoubtedly it means that you cannot consider on Thursdays and Fridays estimates that have not been considered on a previous day. But as, on Thursday and Friday, the Speaker leaves the chair without motion put, it is always competent, when there has been no supply, to make a motion that the Speaker do leave the chair, which then leaves open all the rights and privileges that belong to any member to make a speech or move a motion in amendment. Obviously that was what was meant, but if there is a doubt there is no point to-night in taking up time discussing it.

speechtext: I think we had better hold to the rules as we have understood them heretofore. I hope the Prime Minister will not press the matter this evening.

subtopic: COMMITTEES OF SUPPLY AND WAYS AND MEANS BEFORE ADDRESS AGREED TO
speechtext:
I notice that standing order No. 28 has been interpreted by some in the way the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has construed it, but as a matter of fact I am perfectly certain that that was not the intention of the order at all. In the old days you could not go into supply on any day of the week without a motion, and of course that gave an opportunity to every member to move an amendment, to air grievances, and so on. That was considered as perhaps delaying the busi-

The Address-Mr. Brown

ness of the house too much, and when this clause was put in it was for the purpose of enabling the government to go into supply, without motion, on Thursdays and Fridays, to avoid that difficulty. Then, in order to satisfy the members of the house, it was provided that no items should be taken up on Thursdays and Fridays that had not been already before the committee on some other day; but there was never any intention of taking away from the government the power to move into supply on Thursdays and Fridays in the ordinary way, making a motion which could be debated in the usual manner. I admit that it is possible to interpret the order as some hon. members have interpreted it, but I am perfectly certain that such was not the intention of the order in the first instance; and I submit to the house that it is carrying the argument rather far to say that on Thursdays and Fridays an ordinary motion to go into supply cannot be made by the government, to which motion any hon. member can move an amendment, or debate, or under which he may raise any grievance he may have, as he would on any other day of the week. It is not taking away any privileges from any member of the house if the government has the power to move, in the ordinary way, to go into supply on Thursdays and Fridays, and I am sure that this was the original intention of the rule. Perhaps the wording of the rule was somewhat defective; it was not made as plain as it might have been.

speechtext:
Is it any wonder, if that be true, and I do not think there is any reason to doubt it, that the revenues of our municipalities and provincial governments have been so reduced that it has been absolutely necessary for them to appeal for help?
The Prime Minister quoted many figures the other day to show that general trade conditions are improving. I am not disposed to question those figures; they may be perfectly correct. But I want to emphasize the point made last night by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) that the improvement has not yet reached the farmer. I listened in a few days ago to a conversation among a group of farmers, and the consensus of opinion was that conditions are worse today in that old settled oommunity in southern Manitoba than they had ever been-worse than in the hardest pioneer days through which we passed more than fifty years ago. One of the difficulties facing the people to-day is not onty that municipal and provincial revenues have been reduced, but there is a tremendous personal burden resting upon the farmers. The municipalities and provincial governments naturally cannot get' revenue when the source of that revenue has almost completely dried up. The great problem that confronts us to-day is, what are we to do with that great burden of debt? We have our debt adjustment boards, I think in all three provinces, certainly in Manitoba; but up to the present all the authority that has been given to them is to' secure a delay of proceedings, to prevent creditors from taking immediate drastic action. There are those who tell us that these debt adjustment boards are doing more harm than good, that they are drying up the sources of credit so that farmers cannot borrow a dollar. I am not yet prepared to adopt that view. But there can be no question that these methods cannot be continued indefinitely; at some time we must have a showdown.
What is to be done? I fully appreciate the difficulties of the situation, I fully appreciate the fact that we cannot divide debtors and creditors into two distinct classes and say to one class: You must forego the debts that are due you from the other class. I fully appreciate the fact that the loan companies are largely financed with the money of men and women who have put their life savings into these companies. I appreciate the difficulty, but there is a problem that the people of Canada must face at some time. Much is being said to-day about the farmers' need of

short term and intermediate credit. In my judgment there is nothing that would justify a farmer in borrowing money to-day except to meet some extreme emergency or to refund a debt at a lower rate of interest. There is no single agricultural activity into which a farmer can enter that would warrant his borrowing a single dollar with any hope of making sufficient profit to repay the principal with interest. That is the situation that confronts the people of western Canada to-day.
I want to refer now to the wheat agreement. This agreement is being enthusiastically advocated in some quarters and strenuously opposed in others. I shall try to speak moderately, but I will say this, that I look upon it with a great deal of fear. My fear is that an agreement of this kind, instead of remedying the difficulty, will simply encourage the importing countries in the uneconomic policies that they are pursuing. To try to meet one economic ill, or something that has resulted from uneconomic policies, by adopting another plan of doubtful economic wisdom is to my mind a very uncertain experiment.
Granting for the moment, however, that the scheme be theoretically sound, it seems to me that the difficulties involved in putting it into practical force are almost insuperable. I asked the Prime Minister when he was speaking on the subject what steps the government were taking to give effect to the agreement. His reply was to the effect that no steps were necessary at the moment, that there would foe no need to do anything until there was an indication that the quota would be exceeded. I cannot see how the agreement which he has made can be carried out unless the government is prepared to take charge of the whole thing, the buying and the selling of the wheat. Not that I am particularly in favour of that, but I do not see how it is possible to give effect to the agreement unless they do that. Are we to go on simply in a haphazard way until the time comes when the quota has been almost reached and then have the government step in and take control? It seems to me that would be absolutely unfair to the different exporting countries. Certainly the matter of export comes within the jurisdiction of this government.
When we come to deal with the question of reducing acreage or putting the individual quota back to the farm the difficulties seem to me to be still more insuperable. That, of course, must come within the jurisdiction of provincial governments. Various propositions have been advanced, I know, but there has been no scheme advanced so far as I have heard that is not open to many grave

The Address-Mr. Brown
objections. I know the prairie premiers went home from the recent conference with the intention of making an investigation into the situation and deciding on action later. When they make that investigation, here is what they will find: they will find that for certain reasons there will be a very large reduction in acreage. They wild find that there are many districts, in which drought conditions have prevailed for a number of years, where large areas of land will not be cropped for the reason that the owners of that land will not furnish seed. I know that condition prevailed to some extent last year. They will find that there are many farmers owning their own land who will not be able to buy seed, and that the municipalities and provincial governments will not be in a position to furnish them with seed. For that reason large areas of land will not be put under cultivation. They will find also that the menace of grasshoppers will make very doubtful the wisdom of venturing to any great extent into the sowing of wheat.
Sometimes we are told that farming is a gamble. I do not like to hear that word used in this connection, because it confuses the minds of men as to what gambling really is, but it is a term frequently used. I think we can say, however, that there are many districts in which the grasshopper menace is so great that it would seem that a man would be almost as wise to throw his seed wheat into the sea as to put it into the ground, and for that reason I think they will find that many farmers in the infested districts will act on that principle in some measure and will not risk a very large acreage. They will find also that the conditions through which wc have passed in recent years, and particularly in the last year, have so reduced the supply of feed that there will be many horses found dead all over the prairies. I know that just at Christmas time a certain gentleman told me, in regard to a particular part of my own constituency, that in a seven mile drive he counted eight dead horses. Just before I left home I was told of a man who had lost four horses, and the reports that come to us indicate that hundreds of horses will die during the present winter. With these conditions prevailing-and they do prevail; I am not making any exaggerated statement-I think the prairie premiers will find that it is a matter of very doubtful wisdom to speak of acreage reduction at the present time. Indeed I think they will be very glad to find an opportunity to drop the whole thing.
Now I should like to make a few comments with regard to some of the speeches that have
been made throughout the country. The Prime Minister made a speech in Toronto to which my right hon. leader referred. I did not see as full an account of that speech as did the right hon. leader of the opposition, but I was very much surprised at one brief statement which I read. Speaking of the Laurier preference the Prime Minister was reported as saying that for thirty-five years successive governments have endeavoured to correct the injury that was done to Canadian trade. Those may not be the exact words, but the effect of his remark was that for thirty-five years successive governments had endeavoured to correct the injury that was done to Canada. It seems to me that was a very strange statement to make, when we remember that some of these governments, representing certainly a large proportion of the Canadian people, did not believe that any injury had been done to Canada by those preferences which were granted to Great Britain.
Why will not hon. gentlemen opposite try to get our point of view? We get their point very easily. Their point of view is that the greatest crime that a man can commit is to bring some cheap goods into Canada. We do not hold to that principle. We believe that it would be quite possible to bring some cheap goods into Canada for the benefit of Canadians. Wherefore why should we wlm hold that view consider that an injury had been done to Canada by the preferences granted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier?
The Prime Minister was also wrong when he said that successive governments had endeavoured to correct this so called injury. My understanding is that successive governments did not endeavour to do so. Why should the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, which was in power until 1911, endeavour to correct this so called damage? In my judgment there is no evidence that any such endeavours were made.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
evidently has not read the last memorandum from Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I shall refer to that in a moment. Neither did the government of the present leader of the opposition make any endeavour to correct that so called injury.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman read the proceedings of the 1923 economic conference?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will speak about that. It is true that the Prime Minister, by referring to those things which he has just mentioned,
The Address-Mr. Brown

in his speech defending the Ottawa agreements did, by partial quotations, by statements taken apart from their context and apart from the circumstances under which they were spoken, seem to convince himself, and endeavoured to convince the people, that these governments had tried to correct this so called injury. There is one thing, however, that Liberal governments never did, or else I am greatly mistaken. They never endeavoured to force Great Britain to change her fiscal policy. I think that is a statement that cannot be contradicted, in spite of those things to which the Prime Minister referred so frequently in the course of his remarks, and to which he has now directed our attention. I say again that unless I am tremendously mistaken, and have been mistaken all these years, no Liberal government ever endeavoured to force Great Britain to change her fiscal policy.
That is what hon. gentlemen opposite say they have done. In my judgment there is no warrant for the Prime Minister to say, "We have succeeded where others have failed." Hon. gentlemen opposite say they induced Great Britain to change her fiscal policy; that is the boast that has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite in the last few years. I am not so sure that they will be always glad to boast of that fact. There may be some reason at the moment to believe that Canadian producers of farm products are receiving some benefit in the British market, but mark this: the British agriculturists have tasted blood. They have tasted protection; they are demanding more, and under the present Minister of Agriculture they are being encouraged to demand more. It is true that in the meantime he is being held back by the Ottawa agreements, but there is every reason to believe he regards those as only temporary. At the present time he does not hesitate to place duties upon empire products that are not included in the agreement. There is every reason to believe that at the very first opportunity he will yield to the demand of the British agriculturist for more protection. That is the situation. Then, I read the following from the Winnipeg Free Press of January 16, 1934:
These plans were exposed to general view in a speech Mr. Elliott delivered recently in the south of England to the National Federation of Young Farmers' Clubs. He spoke about the government's anxiety to "improve agriculture" in Great Britain. "We have taken some drastic steps," he said, "but they are nothing to the steps we are going to take in the immediate future." Mr. Elliott then said:
If we are going to live on our own resources we need to know how to do it. Unless the
[Mr. Brown.1
farmers of this country can produce food all this movement will be stopped, but it will not stop until we have had a lot of terribly nasty food at extraordinary high prices, because we are determined to make it go, and will not admit defeat for a long time. It is up to you to see that the young people know a lot about farming, because it is up to them to produce the food in the future.
Let us make no mistake; as I have said, British agriculturists have tasted blood and they are going to demand more. At that time will hon. members who have boasted that the Prime Minister induced Great Britain to change her fiscal policy be as pleased as they seem to have been in the past? The situation is very well stated in these words:
British agricultural protectionism dates from the time when the Canadian government, leading the dominions, asked Great Britain to put duties on foreign foodstuffs. Having tasted protection against foreign competition, the British farmers want protection against empire competition too, and they are being officially encouraged.
When I was preparing my remarks I was not aware that the matter with which we have dealt all afternoon would be up for discussion. I did not take any part in the debate this afternoon, but at this time I will venture just a few words. When I read the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) I was struck with one phrase; he spoke about unethical methods of carrying on business. My attention was attracted by his remarks concerning millers and their relation to the bakers, and they brought to my mind a story about a man who was appearing before a magistrate for driving his car recklessly. Defending himself, he said: " I tooted and tooted and tooted." The magistrate replied: "Why did you not stop your car?" "Well," he said, " that is one on me; I never thought of that." That man never thought of doing the obvious thing. I wondered whether this government would be willing to do the obvious thing and, instead of tooting and tooting and tooting, take steps to correct the evils which naturally grow up under the protective system from which we are suffering to-day. That is all I wish bo say in this connection at the moment.
Some hon. members have been making speeches throughout the country, and I am sorry there are not more of them, particularly those from Manitoba, in their seats. Not only have the greater lights been talking, but some of the lesser lights have been making speeches. I do not use the term "lesser lights" in any offensive manner, because I realize that some of the so-called lesser lights have in them the possibility of becoming

The Address-Mr. Brown
bright and shining lights. Among those hon. members I would not give second place to the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis).
It would seem that this hon. member has been making speeches, and the point he has been trying to impress upon his hearers is that he is not a high tariff man. I read the following:
Mr. Erick F. Willis, M.P. for Souris Manitoba, was delightfully frank in his address to the Conservative Business Men's Club in Toronto.
Mr. Willis told his audience-and it must have been something of a shock to most of those present-that he represented the new type of Conservative which "makes the party a young man's party" and which does not believe in high tariffs and "all the things which historically the party was supposed to stand for."
Well, here is a new party. The province of Manitoba seems to be destined to be closely connected with new parties. In a large measure the personnel of the Progressive party came from Manitoba.
