speechtext:
I have no apologies to
make, so far as that is concerned. The leader of the C.C.F. is also from Manitoba, and now we have a new Conservative party organized in that province. I imagine the hon. members from Manitoba and the rural members from Saskatchewan will be glad to join this party because not one of them would go out into any constituency in Manitoba and defend high tariffs. Let me say to these hon. members that when they come face to face with the electors they will not be asked whether they are in favour of high or low tariffs. They will be asked: " Are you in favour of the tariffs of this government?" That will be the question, not the question whether tariffs are high or low. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) stated in the course of his address: "We will 'be told that the tariffs are high. We admit they are high." Well, they admit they are high, and yet these hon. members from Manitoba are going across the country stating that they do not believe in high tariffs. When I read this statement in the press I begin to wonder just what the attitude of these men really is.
There are motions of want of confidence in the government now before the house. In his motion the right hon. leader of the opposition states that the government has lost the confidence of the country and I believe he stated there was reason to believe they had lost confidence in themselves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not that the government has lost confidence, but that " Your Excellency's present advisers " have lost confidence. Under the British North America Act his advisers are the whole of the privy council, and that means that they have a lack of confidence in themselves.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wondered when I read
about the new party whether they also had not lost the confidence of some of those members who had hitherto been their supporters. However my mind was disabused of that point when the hon. member for Souris sent me the usual documents to be signed in the fixing of pairs. I found that he still paired with me, and is in support of and not in opposition to the government. So that while hon. members opposite talk a great deal about not believing in high tariffs they still support the tariffs which have been imposed by this government. Let me ask hon. gentlemen opposite this question:	Are they in
favour of a duty of twenty-five per cent on agricultural machinery? That is a question they will have to answer. Are they in favour of what was done as a result of the imperial conference, namely the placing of a twenty-five per cent duty on cream separators, and a duty on barbed wire? I would not object to carrying on a campaign with these gentlemen; they would never get away with some of the statements they are trying to put over on the people.
It was my intention to make a few comments concerning the speech made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel). I agree in very large measure with the speech that he made, but he also is in somewhat the same position as some other hon. gentlemen. He told us of the difficulties of the farmer and stated that the farmer had to have a large equipment with which to carry on his work, just as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) did two or three years ago, when he put on Hansard a splendid list of the implements that a farmer had to buy. But the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, like other hon. gentlemen, will still continue to support a government that imposes high tariffs which result in keeping agricultural machinery and all the equipment which the farmer must have at a higher price.
We can only meet the present situation, Mr. Speaker, and this will not bring us immediate relief, by first of all taking a step in the right direction. I know that times are going to be difficult. I do not think that there is anything this government can do, or a government of hon. gentlemen to my left,
Questions

or a government even of this party, that will bring immediate relief. But we can set our faces in the right direction. The last three or four years we have not been going in the right direction. We must make a rightabout face and take steps at once to put into effect the principles that will remove the restrictions from trade and allow trade to move freely between the nations of the world. Not until then will any such methods as are being attempted to-day bring about any effective measure of relief.
There was another matter to which I was going to refer, but I see that my time has almost expired, and I shall have to defer my remarks until another occasion.

understand that it is agreeable to the ministry and all sides of the house that the debate be now adjourned and that we call it a day. I accordingly move that the debate be now adjourned.
